title: Jenkins for Mobile
subtitle: iOS signing, archives, Gradle builds, store upload

blocks.text: Jenkins is a server that runs the same commands you would type in Terminal, on a machine that is not your laptop, every time someone asks or something changes. Everything else is detail on top of that.
What a mobile build pipeline does
Git push or "Build" click*→*Jenkins controller*→*Mac / Linux agent*→*checkout*→*dependencies*→*sign*→*compile*→*.ipa / .apk / .aab*→*TestFlight, Firebase, Play*→*Slack message
Xcode's **Product → Archive → Distribute App** is the same chain, done by hand with buttons. Your job is to turn each button press into a command, then put the commands in a Jenkins job.
Eight nouns cover almost everything you will read in the UI or a log.

rows: The Jenkins server itself: web UI, job config, schedule, history. Older docs call it "master".
Can be Linux. It should not do the builds.
A machine that does the work. Connects to the controller over SSH or an inbound connection.
iOS needs a **macOS** agent with Xcode. Android can build on Linux or Mac.
A slot on an agent. 2 executors = 2 builds at the same time on that machine.
Two iOS archives in parallel on one Mac fight over CPU, DerivedData and the keychain. Many teams use 1 executor per Mac.
A tag on an agent, such as `mac` or `android`. Jobs ask for a label, not a machine name.
`agent { label 'mac-xcode26' }` lets you add a new Xcode on a new Mac without breaking old jobs.
A saved recipe: where the code is, what to run, what to keep.
Your four jobs plus the Release folder.
One execution of a job. Has a number, a result, a log.
`$BUILD_NUMBER` is often used as the app's build number.
The folder on the agent where the repo is checked out for that job.
A file the build asks Jenkins to keep: .ipa, .apk, .aab, dSYMs, mapping.txt.
Stored on the controller's disk. Keep few.

rows: Forms in the UI. "Execute shell" boxes hold the commands. Config is stored only on the server.
Old and simple. Hard to review, no history of who changed what. Common in older mobile setups.
The recipe is code (a `Jenkinsfile`), typed in the UI or loaded from Git.
Today's default. Stages show up as a visual strip.
Scans a repo and creates one pipeline per branch or pull request that has a Jenkinsfile.
PR builds and per-branch builds without manual jobs.
A container for jobs, with its own permissions and credentials.
Your `Release` folder. Release credentials can be scoped to it so debug jobs cannot read them.
Scans a whole GitHub or Bitbucket organisation.

blocks.text: The life of one build

items: **Trigger.** A person clicks Build, a webhook arrives from Git, a timer fires, or another job finishes.
**Queue.** Jenkins looks for an agent with the right label and a free executor.
**Workspace.** The agent checks out the repo into the job's workspace.
**Steps.** Shell commands run one after another. A non-zero exit code fails the build at that line.
**Post.** Archive artifacts, publish reports, send a message, clean up.
**Result.** SUCCESS, UNSTABLE, FAILURE, ABORTED or NOT_BUILT.

A parameterised job shows a form before it starts. Common mobile parameters: branch, build type (debug / release), environment (QA / UAT / prod), upload yes or no, release notes. Each parameter becomes an environment variable in shell steps (`$BRANCH`) and `params.BRANCH` in a Jenkinsfile.

blocks.text: Ways to look at a pipeline run

items: **Stage View**: the grid of stages by build on the job page, with time per stage. First place to see which stage got slower.
**Pipeline Graph View** (plugin, the current default look): the run as a graph, with logs per step.
**Pipeline Steps** link on a build: every step with its own log. Fast way to jump to the failing `sh`.
**Blue Ocean**: an older alternative UI. It still works where installed but gets no new features.
**Console Output**: the whole log. "View as plain text" for searching and copying.

blocks.text: Git details that matter on CI

rows: `depth: 1` fetches only the latest commit. Fast, but `git describe`, commit-count build numbers and "changes since last tag" stop working.
A bare clone kept on the agent; new workspaces borrow objects from it, so a first checkout takes seconds.
`git clean -fdx` removes everything untracked, including `Pods/` and build output. `git clean -fd` keeps ignored files. Choose on purpose.
Both need to be switched on in the checkout step, and both need credentials. A missing LFS pull shows as tiny text files where images should be.
Jenkins checks out a commit, not a branch. Scripts that run `git branch --show-current` get nothing; use `$GIT_BRANCH` or the parameter.
Pushing a tag back from CI needs write credentials and `sshagent`. Keep that to release jobs.

blocks.text: A Jenkinsfile is the build recipe as a text file in the repo. Changes go through pull requests, and every branch can carry the recipe that builds it.
Anatomy (declarative syntax)
Each block

rows: `any`, `none`, `label`, or a Docker image (Android only; there is no macOS in Docker). A stage can override it.
Always set a timeout. A build waiting on a hidden keychain dialog otherwise holds an executor for ever.
The form updates only **after** the first run that contains the new parameter.
`credentials('id')` for a username/password also creates `NAME_USR` and `NAME_PSW`.
Stage names are what you see in the UI strip. One clear job per stage makes red builds easy to place.
`always, success, failure, unstable, aborted, changed, fixed, cleanup`. Put keychain deletion in `always`.
Good for lint + unit tests on separate agents. Not for two archives on one Mac.
"Promote to production?" Put it outside an agent so it does not hold an executor while waiting.

blocks.text: Nine out of ten red iOS builds on CI are signing. Xcode hides it behind "Automatically manage signing". On Jenkins you have to know the pieces.
The five pieces

rows: Secret half of a key pair. Created on a Mac when someone makes a Certificate Signing Request.
Keychain of the Mac that made it. Exported with the certificate as a `.p12` file.
Apple's statement "this public key belongs to team X". Types: **Apple Development** (run on registered devices from Xcode) and **Apple Distribution** (ad hoc, TestFlight, App Store). Valid 1 year.
developer.apple.com → Certificates. Download as `.cer`. Useless without the private key.
Bundle identifier plus the capabilities turned on (Push, App Groups, Sign in with Apple, …).
A signed file that ties together: one App ID + certificates allowed to sign + (for development and ad hoc) the device list + entitlements. Valid 1 year.
`.mobileprovision`. On disk under `~/Library/MobileDevice/Provisioning Profiles/`; Xcode 16 and later also use `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/UserData/Provisioning Profiles/`.
The list of special permissions the binary claims. Must be a subset of what the profile grants.

blocks.text: How they fit
Private key + certificate (.p12)*signs*App binary*checked against*Profile (App ID, certs, devices, entitlements)*embedded in*.ipa

At install time iOS checks: is the profile signed by Apple, does the bundle ID match, was the app signed by a certificate listed in the profile, is this device listed (development and ad hoc only), are all claimed entitlements granted.

lessons.title: Profile types and what they are for

rows: Registered only (100 per device type per year)
QA builds through Firebase App Distribution or a link
Internal apps under the Enterprise Program

blocks.text: The new method names arrived with Xcode 15.3. Old names still work with a deprecation warning. Your agent runs a recent Xcode (your Mac has 26.0.1), so use the new names.

**Your app has several targets, so several profiles.** The Podfile lists the main app plus `NotificationServices` and `BBPushTemplateExtension`, and the repo has a `BBLiveActivityExtension` folder. Every extension has its own bundle ID and needs its own profile of the same type. A missing extension profile is the classic "works for the app, export fails" error.
Automatic or manual signing on CI

rows: Install the .p12 and each .mobileprovision on the agent. Targets name their profile.
Pass `-allowProvisioningUpdates` and an App Store Connect API key; Xcode creates and downloads what it needs.
Predictable. The build never changes anything in the Apple account.
No profile files to carry. New devices and capabilities are picked up.
Someone has to refresh profiles when devices or capabilities change, and every year.
The key needs a role that can manage certificates; a build can create certificates until the account limit is hit.

blocks.text: Do it in three passes: by hand in Xcode so you know the result, in Terminal so you know the commands, then in Jenkins so nobody has to type them.
Android is simpler: one tool (Gradle), one secret file (the keystore), and it builds on Linux. The team already has two jobs; this is how they work inside.
Outputs

rows: Installable, signed with the auto-generated debug key
Installable, signed with your keystore, shrunk by R8
App bundle for Play. Play builds per-device APKs from it. Not installable directly.
R8 name map; needed to read release crash stacks

blocks.text: With flavors the task name is `assemble<Flavor><BuildType>`, for example `assembleProdRelease`. List what exists with `./gradlew tasks --all` or `./gradlew :app:tasks`.

rows: File holding one or more private keys. Has a store password.
Which key inside the store, and its password.
The key CI signs with. Play checks it, strips it, and re-signs with the app signing key.
Held by Google under Play App Signing. If the upload key leaks or is lost it can be reset; the app signing key cannot.

`~/.android/debug.keystore`, created automatically. Each machine has its own, so SHA-1 based services (Google Sign-In, Maps, Firebase) fail on CI debug builds unless the team shares one debug keystore.

blocks.text: The property names (`KEY_STORE_FILE`, `STORE_PASSWD`, `KEY_ALIAS`, `KEY_PASSWD`, `VERSION_CODE`), the `Regular` flavor and the `Flutter` folder are what your `app/build.gradle` and `settings.gradle` use. A `-P` value overrides the same key in `gradle.properties`. For a debug job you can drop the four signing properties and the `withCredentials` block: the dev keystore from the repo is used. Credential IDs and the agent label are placeholders, `BUILD_NUMBER` as version code is only an example (your Play version code is already above 1173, so a Jenkins counter starting at 1 would be rejected), and I have not seen the two Android job configs.
What the agent needs

items: **JDK** that the Android Gradle Plugin version wants (AGP 8 needs JDK 17). Set `JAVA_HOME`. Do not rely on whatever `java` is first on the PATH.
**Android SDK** with command-line tools, the right `platforms;android-NN` and `build-tools`. Accept licences once: `yes | sdkmanager --licenses`.
**Gradle wrapper** in the repo (`./gradlew`) so the Gradle version is fixed by the repo, not by the machine.
**Memory.** R8 and Kotlin compile are hungry. An out-of-memory kill shows as "Gradle build daemon disappeared unexpectedly".
`local.properties` is not in Git. On CI use `ANDROID_HOME` (older name `ANDROID_SDK_ROOT`) instead.

blocks.text: Useful Gradle switches on CI

rows: No background process left behind on a shared agent. On a dedicated agent keeping the daemon is faster.
Reuse task outputs from earlier builds (or a remote cache).
Uploads a build report to Gradle's service. Check company policy first.
Proves the build needs nothing new from the network.
Skip a task. Use for speed in debug jobs, not to hide a failing check.

blocks.code:
apksigner verify --print-certs app-release.apk      # who signed it
aapt2 dump badging app-release.apk | head -3        # package, versionCode, versionName
keytool -list -v -keystore upload.jks -alias upload # key fingerprints and expiry
bundletool build-apks --bundle=app.aab --output=app.apks --mode=universal   # make an installable from an .aab

blocks.text: `apksigner`, `aapt2` and `zipalign` live in the SDK's `build-tools/<version>/` folder and are not on the PATH by default (they are not on yours). Call them by full path or add that folder to PATH on the agent. `bundletool` is a separate download.

blocks.text: APK signature schemes

rows: Signs files one by one. Needed only below Android 7; your minSdk is 24, so it is not needed.
Signs the whole APK. Faster install, tamper-evident.
A separate `.idsig` file for incremental install.

blocks.text: `apksigner verify -v app.apk` prints which schemes are present. Editing an APK after signing (even re-zipping) breaks v2 and later.
R8, minify and the rules file

items: `minifyEnabled true` (your `release` and `beta` types) runs R8: removes unused code, renames what is left.

Code reached by reflection, JSON models and some SDKs need keep rules in `proguard-rules.pro`. A crash that happens only in release or beta and names a class like `a.b.c` is nearly always a missing rule.
That is the reason a `beta` type exists: it is debug behaviour with release shrinking, so the missing rule shows up before production.

blocks.text: Instrumented checks and emulators on CI

items: Device checks need a device. Options: an emulator on the agent (needs hardware acceleration, so not inside most cloud VMs), Gradle Managed Devices (Gradle creates and starts the emulator), or a device farm such as Firebase Test Lab.
Start an emulator headless: `emulator -avd ci_api34 -no-window -no-audio -no-snapshot`, then wait for `adb shell getprop sys.boot_completed` to print 1.
Turn off animations on the device for stable UI runs: `adb shell settings put global animator_duration_scale 0` (and the two other scale settings).

blocks.text: Play rules that break release jobs

items: **Target API level.** Since 31 August 2026 new apps and updates must target Android 16 (API 36) or higher. Your target is 36, so the app meets it. The level rises every year.

**16 KB page size.** Apps targeting Android 15 or later must support 16 KB memory pages on 64-bit devices. From 1 February 2027 Play will not accept updates that do not. NDK r28 and later (yours is r28) and AGP 8.5.1 and later (yours is 8.13.2) build 16 KB aligned by default, so the usual blocker is an old prebuilt `.so` inside a third-party SDK. Check a build with `zipalign -c -P 16 -v 4 app.apk`.
**Data safety form and permissions declarations** are filled in Play Console, not by CI, but an upload can be blocked until they are current.

blocks.text: Your apps are native hosts that embed a Flutter **module** (add-to-app). CI never runs `flutter build ipa` or `flutter build apk`; the native build pulls Flutter in.

lessons.title: iOS: how the module gets in

items: `flutter pub get` in `FlutterFrameworks` downloads Dart packages and generates the hidden `.ios/` folder with `Flutter/podhelper.rb`.
The Podfile loads that helper and calls `install_all_flutter_pods(flutter_application_path)`. That adds the Flutter engine, plugin pods and a script phase to the app target.
During `xcodebuild`, the script phase runs `xcode_backend.sh`, which compiles the Dart code for the current configuration: JIT for Debug, AOT (ahead of time, optimised) for Release and Profile.

blocks.text: **Build mode follows the Xcode configuration name.** Flutter decides debug / profile / release from the configuration. Custom names (your Podfile mentions `Beta` and `Flutter Release`) must be mapped, otherwise Flutter can pick the wrong mode or stop with "Unknown FLUTTER_BUILD_MODE". Check how the project sets `FLUTTER_BUILD_MODE` before adding a new configuration on CI.
The other way: prebuilt frameworks

`flutter build ios-framework --output=some/dir` produces `Flutter.xcframework`, `App.xcframework` and one per plugin, for Debug, Profile and Release. The host app links them like any binary. Trade-off: iOS developers and CI need no Flutter SDK for native-only work and builds are faster, but someone must rebuild and version the frameworks whenever Dart code changes. Your repo uses the source route (podhelper), not this one.
Android: two matching routes

rows: `settings.gradle` evaluates the module's `.android/include_flutter.groovy`; app depends on `project(':flutter')`
Flutter SDK on the agent; `flutter pub get` before Gradle
`flutter build aar` writes a local Maven repo; the app depends on the published AARs
Flutter SDK only in the job that builds the AAR

blocks.text: Your Android app uses the **source** route: `settings.gradle` evaluates `Flutter/.android/include_flutter.groovy`. Both platforms therefore need the Flutter SDK on the build machine.
CI rules for Flutter

items: **Pin the Flutter version.** Your Mac has 3.41.4. The agent must match what the team develops on, or generated code and engine differ. Use FVM (`.fvmrc` in the repo, `fvm flutter pub get`) or a fixed SDK path per version, and print `flutter --version` at the top of every build.
**Commit `pubspec.lock`** for apps and modules so CI resolves the same package versions. Use `flutter pub get --enforce-lockfile` to fail when the lock is out of date.

**Generated code.** If `.g.dart` files are committed (they are in your repos), CI must not regenerate them. If a team does not commit them, CI runs `dart run build_runner build --delete-conflicting-outputs` before the native build.

**Dart defines.** Environment switches passed as `--dart-define` in a pure Flutter app have no direct equivalent in add-to-app; they travel through the Xcode build setting `DART_DEFINES` or through the native side. Know which one your app uses before adding an "environment" parameter.
**Caches.** `~/.pub-cache` and Flutter's `bin/cache` are safe to keep between builds and save minutes. Do not wipe them in cleanup scripts.
**Checks for the Dart side.** `flutter analyze` and the Dart unit tests can run on a cheap Linux agent in parallel with the Mac archive.

blocks.text: Dart symbols and obfuscation

A pure Flutter app can build with `--obfuscate --split-debug-info=build/symbols`, which renames Dart symbols and writes symbol files needed to read Dart stack traces later (`flutter symbolize`, or upload to the crash service). In add-to-app the same options travel as build settings read by the Flutter build script. If your team turns obfuscation on, the symbol folder becomes one more artifact to archive with dSYMs and mapping.txt; without it, Dart crash stacks from that build are unreadable.

rows: Performance work on a real device

`Release` and `Flutter Release`. No device-side `FLUTTER_BUILD_MODE` is set in your project, so Flutter derives the mode from the configuration name, which must contain debug, profile or release. `Beta` contains none of them, so a Beta archive needs an explicit `FLUTTER_BUILD_MODE`; I did not build it to confirm.

blocks.text: A debug-mode Flutter build cannot be launched from the home screen on a recent iOS device without a debugger attached, which is one more reason tester builds must be release mode.
A build nobody can install is not finished. These are the upload steps that follow Export and Build.

blocks.text: App Store Connect API key

Created in App Store Connect → Users and Access → Integrations. You get a **Key ID**, an **Issuer ID** and a one-time download `AuthKey_KEYID.p8`. It replaces Apple ID + password + two-factor codes, which cannot work unattended. Store the .p8 as a Jenkins *Secret file*, the two IDs as *Secret text*.

rows: Set by humans in the repo, on the release branch.
Must increase on every upload. Let CI set it.

blocks.text: Sources for the build number: Jenkins `BUILD_NUMBER` (simple; resets if the job is recreated, and two jobs have two counters), `git rev-list --count HEAD` (same on every machine; breaks with shallow clones and differs per branch), or a timestamp like `2611121452`. Pick one for release jobs and never change it.
Telling people
Good messages carry: app, branch, commit subject, build number, install link, who started it. Useful extras: a QR code of the install link, and a comment on the Jira ticket with the build number.
A release flow most teams converge on

items: Cut `release_8.40.0` from develop. Bump the version in that branch.
Every push to the branch builds a release candidate and sends it to TestFlight internal / Play internal.
QA signs off a specific build number.
That same binary is promoted (TestFlight → App Store review; Play internal → production). Never rebuild for production: promote what was tested.
Tag the commit `v8.40.0-b253`, keep dSYMs and mapping.txt, merge the branch back.
Phased release / staged rollout, watch crash-free rate, halt if it drops.

lessons.title: Apple rules that reject an upload

rows: Since 28 April 2026 uploads must be built with Xcode 26 or later and an iOS 26 SDK; older builds are refused (ITMS-90725). Since 9 September 2026 apps must also target iOS 13 or later. Apple raises this roughly once a year.
Your Mac has Xcode 26.0.1 and the app targets iOS 14, so both are met. Watch Apple's "Upcoming Requirements" page and upgrade one agent first.
Required since 1 May 2024: the app and listed third-party SDKs must declare approved reasons for certain APIs in `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` (ITMS-91053, ITMS-91061)
Update the SDKs named in the email; add the app's own manifest.
Add the key to Info.plist, even if only a library uses the API.
Build number reused, or version lower than the live one
CI stamps the build number; humans bump the version on the release branch.
Extension version differs from the app's, or an extension's bundle ID is not prefixed by the app's
Stamp all targets together. Your four IDs follow the prefix rule.
Entitlement not in the profile, or a development-signed binary
Export with the `app-store-connect` method and matching profiles.

blocks.text: Most of these arrive as an email after upload, not as a failed Jenkins build. Send the Apple account's notification emails to a shared mailbox so the team sees them.
Review and rollout

items: **App Store review** usually takes about a day. Expedited review exists for urgent fixes. Release can be manual, automatic after approval, or scheduled.
**Phased release (iOS)**: 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50, 100 percent over seven days for automatic updates; can be paused for up to 30 days. Users who update by hand get it at once.
**Staged rollout (Play)**: you pick the percentage and raise it; can be halted. A halted release stays on the phones that already have it.
**Hotfix**: branch from the release tag, fix, bump the patch version, run the same release pipeline. Do not hotfix from develop.
**Kill switch**: risky features behind a remote flag, so "rollback" is a config change and not a store release.

blocks.text: Release notes from Git

blocks.code:
# Commits since the previous tag, one line each
PREV=$(git describe --tags --abbrev=0 HEAD^ 2>/dev/null || true)
git log --no-merges --pretty='- %s (%an)' ${PREV:+$PREV..}HEAD | head -30 > build/notes.txt

# Jira keys mentioned in those commits
git log --pretty=%s ${PREV:+$PREV..}HEAD | grep -oE '[A-Z]+-[0-9]+' | sort -u

blocks.text: Needs a full clone (no shallow depth) and tags fetched. Feed `build/notes.txt` to Firebase with `--release-notes-file`.
Most "it works on my Mac" CI failures are differences between your Mac and the agent. An agent is a Mac someone has to look after.
Setting up a Mac build agent

items: **User.** A dedicated account (often `jenkins`) with auto-login turned on.

**Run the agent inside the logged-in session.** Start it as a **LaunchAgent** (per user, has a GUI session) and not as a LaunchDaemon (system, no session). Keychain access, simulators and codesign behave correctly only in a user session. Agents launched over plain SSH also get a limited session, which is why the temporary-keychain recipe exists.

**Xcode.** Install, open once, accept the licence (`sudo xcodebuild -license accept`), install components (`xcodebuild -runFirstLaunch`), download the iOS platform. Keep two versions side by side as `/Applications/Xcode-26.0.app` and select per job with `DEVELOPER_DIR`. Avoid `sudo xcode-select -s` inside jobs: it changes the whole machine under other running builds.
**Tools.** Homebrew, a pinned Ruby (rbenv) for CocoaPods and fastlane, CocoaPods, Flutter (FVM), JDK and Android SDK if it also builds Android, Firebase CLI.

**PATH.** Jobs do not read your `.zshrc`. Set PATH in the node's configuration (*Node Properties → Environment variables*) or in the Jenkinsfile's `environment`. "command not found: pod" on CI while it works in Terminal is always this.
**Power.** Never sleep: `sudo pmset -a sleep 0 displaysleep 0 disksleep 0`.
**Connect.** Manage Jenkins → Nodes → New Node: remote root directory, labels, number of executors, launch method (SSH from controller, or inbound agent started on the Mac).

blocks.text: Looking after it

rows: Xcode fails in odd ways when the disk is nearly full

Clear `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData`, `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/Archives`, old simulators (`xcrun simctl delete unavailable`), old workspaces. Do not delete `~/.pub-cache`, `~/.gradle/caches` or CocoaPods caches as routine: they are what make builds fast.
Turn off automatic updates; update on a plan, one agent first
Timeouts; check for dialogs through Screen Sharing
Node offline alerts, disk-space monitor (built into Nodes page), queue length

blocks.text: Jenkins administration basics

items: **JENKINS_HOME** holds everything: `jobs/`, `config.xml`, `credentials.xml`, `secrets/`, `plugins/`. Backing it up (with the `secrets` folder, or credentials cannot be decrypted) is backing up Jenkins.
**LTS line.** Your server runs 2.541.3, a Long-Term Support release (three-part number). Weekly releases have two parts. Production servers stay on LTS.
**Plugins.** Update in a batch, on a quiet day, after a backup. Read the security advisories; most Jenkins security problems are plugin problems.
**Safe restart.** `/safeRestart` waits for running builds. `/quietDown` stops new builds from starting before maintenance.
**Script Console.** *Manage Jenkins → Script Console* runs Groovy with full power on the controller. Admin only, and it can read every secret.
**Configuration as Code.** The JCasC plugin loads a YAML file that describes the server; with Job DSL or Multibranch for jobs, a lost server can be rebuilt from Git.
**Controller executors = 0.** Builds should not run on the controller; a build there can read Jenkins' own files.

blocks.text: A mobile CI server holds the keys that can ship code to every customer's phone. Treat it like production.
Credential kinds

rows: One string: a password, API token, key ID
A file: .p12, .p8, keystore, service-account JSON, zip of profiles

blocks.text: Scope

items: **System**: only Jenkins itself (for example to connect agents). Jobs cannot use it.
**Global**: every job on the server.
**Folder**: only jobs inside that folder. Put the App Store key and the upload keystore in the `Release` folder's store so a debug or PR job cannot read them.

blocks.text: Rules

items: No secret in the repo, in a job's shell text, or in a parameter default. Password-type parameters are still visible to anyone who can configure the job.
Bind with `withCredentials` around the smallest block that needs it.
Single-quoted `sh` strings for anything secret (see Jenkinsfile chapter).

Masking is a courtesy: Jenkins replaces the exact secret string in the log with `****`. `base64` of it, or printing it one character per line, gets through. Anyone who can edit a job that uses a credential can extract that credential.
So: who can **configure** jobs, and who can change the Jenkinsfile on a branch that release jobs build, is who can read the keys. Protect release branches and limit Configure permission.
Temporary keychain per build, deleted in `post always`. Secret files are removed by Jenkins when the block ends; copies you made are not.
API keys with the lowest role that works (App Store Connect "App Manager" or "Developer" for uploads, not "Admin").
Rotate when someone with access leaves. Keep a list of every credential ID, what it is, who owns it, when it expires.

blocks.text: Access control

items: Login through company SSO / LDAP, no shared accounts, no anonymous read.
Matrix or Role-based authorization: developers Build + Read, a small group Configure, fewer still Administer.
Personal **API tokens** (User → Security) for scripts, never passwords. CSRF protection (crumbs) stays on.
Jenkins behind HTTPS (yours is) and ideally reachable only on VPN.
**Script approval**: pipelines from Git run in a Groovy sandbox; calls outside the allow-list wait in *In-process Script Approval* for an admin. Approving blindly defeats the sandbox.
Audit Trail plugin or Job Configuration History plugin to see who changed a job.

blocks.text: Supply chain

items: Commit lock files: `Podfile.lock`, `pubspec.lock`, `Gemfile.lock`, Gradle dependency locking or verification metadata.
`pod install`, never `pod update`, on CI. CI installs what the lock file says.
Gradle wrapper checksum (`distributionSha256Sum`) so a tampered Gradle download fails.
Build scripts in pods and Gradle plugins run with the agent's rights; new dependencies deserve a review.

blocks.text: Measure first. Timestamps in the console show which stage owns the minutes. In Xcode, *Product → Perform Action → Build With Timing Summary* (or `-showBuildTimingSummary`) shows where compile time goes.

rows: Do not delete the workspace every build; use `git clean` selectively and keep `Pods/` and DerivedData
Stale state can hide or cause failures. Keep a "clean build" checkbox parameter and a nightly clean build.
None if the comparison is exact
Drop `clean` from `clean archive` on debug jobs
Shallow clone (`depth: 1`), reference repo, sparse checkout
Checkout time on a big repo
Breaks commit-count build numbers and changelog steps
Keep pub, Gradle and CocoaPods caches on the agent
Parallel stages on different agents (analyze, unit tests, archive)
Prebuilt Flutter frameworks / AAR for native-only changes
A second pipeline to build and version them
Faster Mac (Apple silicon with more cores, more RAM)

blocks.text: Reproducible builds

items: Everything that affects the output is pinned in the repo: Xcode version (a `.xcode-version` file), Flutter (`.fvmrc`), Ruby (`.ruby-version`), gems, pods, Gradle wrapper, JDK.
The Jenkinsfile prints all tool versions at the start. When a build breaks "with no code change", diff that block against the last green build.
Same commit + same pins → same app. Build once, promote the same binary through QA to production.

blocks.text: Concurrency traps on a Mac

items: Two jobs changing the keychain search list at once: one loses its identity mid-build. Use `lock('keychain')` or one executor.
Shared `~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData`: use `-derivedDataPath` per workspace.
Shared simulators: create a simulator per build (`xcrun simctl create`) or lock them.
Profiles folder is shared by all jobs; installing by UUID makes that safe.

blocks.text: Ephemeral agents

Instead of one long-lived Mac that drifts, start a clean macOS virtual machine for each build and destroy it after (Tart, Anka, Orka, or EC2 Mac instances). Clean state every time, golden images versioned like code, and secrets never persist on disk. Costs: image upkeep and cold caches (solved with cache volumes). Apple's licence allows two macOS VMs per physical Mac. Android does the same with Docker or Kubernetes agents far more cheaply.
From UI jobs to pipeline as code

items: Copy each Freestyle job's shell steps into scripts in the repo (`ci/ios_archive.sh`). The job now calls one script. Behaviour unchanged, but the steps are in Git.
Write a Jenkinsfile that calls those scripts stage by stage. Run it as a new Pipeline job beside the old one.
Compare outputs (size, entitlements, version) of old and new for a week.
Switch, keep the old job disabled for a release cycle, then delete.
Later: Multibranch for PRs, shared library for common steps, JCasC for the server.

blocks.text: Jenkins and the alternatives

rows: Full control, any workflow, runs inside the company network, no per-minute bill
You maintain server, plugins, Macs; dated UI
YAML in repo, hosted or self-hosted runners
Tight PR integration, marketplace, hosted macOS runners
macOS minutes are expensive; hosted runners start cold
Signing handled by Apple, TestFlight built in
iOS only, limited custom steps, awkward for add-to-app and Android
Ready steps for signing and stores, Flutter-aware
Per-seat or per-minute cost, less control

blocks.text: Observability

items: Track: success rate per job, median and p90 duration, queue wait, time to fix a red main branch, most frequent failure stage.
Sources: the REST API (`/job/NAME/api/json?tree=builds[number,result,duration,timestamp]`), the Prometheus metrics plugin, or OpenTelemetry plugin for per-stage traces.
Classify failures: infrastructure (agent offline, network, disk) versus code. If infrastructure failures are more than a few percent, fix the system before anything else.

blocks.text: Advanced pipeline patterns

items: **Matrix**: `matrix { axes { axis { name 'FLAVOR'; values 'qa','uat','prod' } } }` builds combinations in parallel.
**Build once, sign many**: archive once, then run `-exportArchive` twice with two plists to get an ad hoc and an App Store .ipa from identical code.
**Re-signing**: an existing .ipa can be re-signed with another profile without rebuilding, as long as entitlements still fit.
**Promotion with `input`**: a release pipeline pauses for approval from a named group before the store upload.
**Changeset-driven stages**: `when { changeset 'FlutterFrameworks/**' }` to run Dart checks only when Dart changed.
**Webhook to chat-ops**: a Slack command posts to `buildWithParameters` so QA can request a build of a branch without opening Jenkins.

blocks.text: Search the error text from the console. Read logs from the first error, not the last line: the last line is usually only "exit code 65".
How to debug any red build

items: Which stage is red? That names the tool: git, pod, flutter, security, xcodebuild, gradle, upload.
Open Console Output, search for `error:` (xcodebuild), `FAILURE:` / `What went wrong` (Gradle), `[!]` (CocoaPods).
Compare with the last green build: same agent? same tool versions? what commits are in between (the Changes link)?
Reproduce the failing command on your Mac from a clean clone of the same commit.
If it only fails on the agent, the difference is environment: PATH, Xcode version, keychain, disk, a cached file. Print it (`env | sort`, `which pod`, `df -h`).
Use Replay to add diagnostic lines without committing.

blocks.text: Reading does not make this stick. Each rung is something to do. Ticks are saved in this browser only.

**Safety on the company server.** Reading configs and logs and starting the debug Custom jobs is normal use. Do not edit a shared job, touch anything in `Release`, or add credentials without the owner's go-ahead. Do the experiments on your local Jenkins or a sandbox copy.

questions.q: What is CI/CD in one breath?
questions.a: Continuous Integration: every change is merged often and an automatic build with checks proves it still works. Continuous Delivery: every good build is packaged and ready to release with one decision. Continuous Deployment: that decision is automatic too. Mobile teams usually stop at Delivery because store review and staged rollout need a human.

questions.q: Why not just archive from a developer laptop?
questions.a: Laptops differ: Xcode version, uncommitted changes, personal certificates. A CI build comes from a known commit on a known machine, is repeatable, leaves a log and an artifact, does not block a developer for 20 minutes, and does not depend on one person being at work.

questions.q: Controller, agent, executor: what is the difference?
questions.a: The controller schedules work and serves the UI. An agent is a machine that runs builds. An executor is one build slot on an agent. iOS builds need a macOS agent; the controller can be Linux.

questions.q: Freestyle job or Pipeline job?
questions.a: Freestyle is configured by forms and stored only on the server. Pipeline is code in a Jenkinsfile, reviewed and versioned with the app, with stages, parallelism, restart from stage and per-branch behaviour. New work should be Pipeline.

questions.q: What do the S and W columns on the dashboard mean?
questions.a: S is the status of the last build. W is weather: the share of the last five builds that passed. A job can be green with clouds (passing now, failed recently) or red with sun (just broke).

questions.q: What is an artifact and what is a fingerprint?
questions.a: An artifact is a file a build keeps, like an .ipa. A fingerprint is its MD5 recorded by Jenkins so you can later ask which build produced a file and which other jobs used it.

questions.q: What does UNSTABLE mean?
questions.a: The build completed but something marked it as not fully good, typically failed tests or a quality threshold. It sits between SUCCESS and FAILURE and is shown in yellow.

questions.q: How can a build be triggered?
questions.a: Manually, by webhook from the Git server, by polling Git on a schedule, by timer, by another job finishing, or through the REST API with a user token.

questions.q: What is the H in a Jenkins cron expression?
questions.a: A hash of the job name mapped into the allowed range. H/15 means every 15 minutes at an offset unique to this job, so jobs do not all start in the same second.

questions.q: What is a workspace and should it be wiped every build?
questions.a: The checkout folder for a job on an agent. Wiping gives clean, reproducible builds but is slow. Common practice: keep it for PR and debug builds, wipe for release builds, plus a nightly clean build to catch stale-state problems.

questions.q: Declarative vs scripted pipeline?
questions.a: Declarative has a fixed structure (pipeline, agent, stages, post), is validated before running and is easier to read. Scripted is plain Groovy inside node blocks with full freedom. Use declarative and a script block for the rare complex part.

questions.q: What is the post section for?
questions.a: Steps that run after the stages depending on the result: always, success, failure, unstable, aborted, changed, fixed, cleanup. Cleanup of keychains and notifications belong there because they must run even when a stage fails.

questions.q: How do you pass secrets to a step?
questions.a: Store them in Jenkins Credentials and bind them with withCredentials or the credentials() helper in the environment block. Use them from single-quoted shell strings so the shell, not Groovy, expands them.

questions.q: Why single quotes around sh commands that use secrets?
questions.a: In a double-quoted Groovy string the secret is interpolated into the command text before execution, which can leak through the process list and the log, and Jenkins warns about it. In single quotes the shell reads the variable from its environment.

questions.q: What is a Multibranch Pipeline?
questions.a: A job that scans a repository and creates a pipeline for every branch and pull request containing a Jenkinsfile, removing them when the branch is deleted. It is how PR checks are done.

questions.q: What is a shared library?
questions.a: A separate Git repo of reusable pipeline code. Files under vars become custom steps. It keeps many Jenkinsfiles short and consistent. Version it and pin the version for release pipelines.

questions.q: stash/unstash vs archiveArtifacts?
questions.a: stash moves files between stages or agents inside one run and is discarded afterwards. archiveArtifacts keeps files with the build for people and other jobs to download later.

questions.q: How do you stop two builds from clashing?
questions.a: disableConcurrentBuilds for the same job, the lock step (Lockable Resources) for a shared thing such as a keychain or device, and agent executor count for the whole machine.

questions.q: How do you test a Jenkinsfile change without committing?
questions.a: Replay on an earlier build lets you edit the pipeline text and run it once. The declarative linter validates syntax. For bigger changes use a sandbox copy of the job pointing at a feature branch.

questions.q: Why set a timeout?
questions.a: A hung step, usually a hidden keychain or licence dialog or a stuck network call, would otherwise hold an executor until someone notices, blocking the queue.

questions.q: What does the when directive do?
questions.a: It makes a stage conditional: on a branch, a tag, a parameter value, changed paths, or any expression. Typical use: upload only when the UPLOAD parameter is ticked or the branch is a release branch.

questions.q: How would you add a manual approval before production upload?
questions.a: An input step in its own stage with agent none, with a submitter list limiting who can approve and a timeout so a forgotten build is aborted instead of waiting for ever.

questions.q: Walk through what happens when you Archive in Xcode.
questions.a: Xcode runs the scheme's Archive action, normally the Release configuration, for a generic iOS device. It compiles all targets, signs them, and writes an .xcarchive containing the .app, dSYMs and metadata. Distribute App then re-signs for the chosen method and exports an .ipa.

questions.q: Which commands replace Archive and Distribute?
questions.a: xcodebuild archive with -workspace, -scheme, -destination generic/platform=iOS and -archivePath, then xcodebuild -exportArchive with -archivePath, -exportPath and -exportOptionsPlist.

questions.q: What is in ExportOptions.plist?
questions.a: The distribution method, team ID, signing style, the certificate name, a map of bundle ID to provisioning profile for every target, and options such as symbol upload, bitcode-era settings, thinning and destination (export or upload).

questions.q: What is the difference between .xcarchive and .ipa?
questions.a: The archive is the build result with debug symbols, not installable and not tied to a distribution method. The .ipa is a zip with a Payload folder holding the app signed for one method. One archive can be exported to several .ipa files.

questions.q: Explain certificate, provisioning profile and entitlements.
questions.a: The certificate with its private key proves who signed. The profile, signed by Apple, says this App ID may be signed by these certificates, run on these devices (development and ad hoc), with these entitlements. Entitlements are the capabilities the binary claims and must be allowed by the profile.

questions.q: Development vs ad hoc vs App Store profile?
questions.a: Development: development certificate, registered devices, debuggable. Ad hoc: distribution certificate, registered devices, for testers outside TestFlight. App Store: distribution certificate, no device list, only installable through TestFlight or the store.

questions.q: Why do CI builds need a special keychain?
questions.a: codesign needs the private key from an unlocked keychain in the search list, with permission to use it without a dialog. On a headless agent the login keychain may be locked or prompt. A temporary keychain created, unlocked and granted to codesign for the build solves that and is deleted afterwards.

questions.q: What does set-key-partition-list do?
questions.a: It records which tools may use an imported key without the user confirming. Since macOS Sierra, skipping it makes codesign wait on a dialog, which on CI looks like a hang or errSecInternalComponent.

questions.q: Automatic signing on CI: how?
questions.a: Pass -allowProvisioningUpdates to xcodebuild with an App Store Connect API key through -authenticationKeyPath, -authenticationKeyID and -authenticationKeyIssuerID. Xcode then creates or downloads certificates and profiles. Many teams still prefer manual signing for release jobs because it is predictable.

questions.q: What is an App Store Connect API key and why use it?
questions.a: A .p8 private key with a key ID and issuer ID that authenticates tools to App Store Connect. It replaces Apple ID logins, which need two-factor codes and cannot run unattended, and it can be limited by role.

questions.q: Why -workspace and not -project?
questions.a: CocoaPods creates a workspace that contains the app project and the Pods project. Building only the project misses the pod targets and fails with missing modules.

questions.q: What are dSYMs and why keep them?
questions.a: Debug symbol files that map addresses in a crash report back to function names and lines. Without the dSYM of the exact build (matched by UUID), crash reports are unreadable. Upload them to the crash service and archive them.

questions.q: An app has a notification extension. What changes for signing?
questions.a: Each extension is its own target with its own bundle ID and needs its own App ID and provisioning profile of the same type. ExportOptions.plist must list a profile for each, and versions must match the main app.

questions.q: How do you set the build number on CI?
questions.a: Pass CURRENT_PROJECT_VERSION to xcodebuild if Info.plist uses that build setting, or run agvtool new-version -all, or edit Info.plist with PlistBuddy. Apply it to every target. Use a value that always increases, such as the CI build number.

questions.q: How do you run more than one Xcode on an agent?
questions.a: Install them as separately named apps and choose per job with the DEVELOPER_DIR environment variable. Avoid xcode-select -s inside jobs because it changes the machine for other builds running at the same time.

questions.q: What is exit code 65 from xcodebuild?
questions.a: A generic build failure. It carries no detail; find the first line with "error:" earlier in the log. If output is piped through a formatter, keep the raw log too.

questions.q: How do you upload to TestFlight from CI?
questions.a: Export with the app-store-connect method, then xcrun altool --upload-app with the API key, or set destination to upload in the export options, or use fastlane pilot. The build then goes through Apple processing before testers see it.

questions.q: What is fastlane match?
questions.a: A way to share signing assets: certificates and profiles are stored encrypted in a private Git repo or bucket, and every developer and CI machine installs the same ones with one command in read-only mode. It ends "works on my machine" signing.

questions.q: Can you re-sign an .ipa without rebuilding?
questions.a: Yes. Unzip, replace embedded.mobileprovision, run codesign with the new identity and matching entitlements on frameworks, extensions and then the app, and zip again. xcodebuild -exportArchive from the same archive is the cleaner route.

questions.q: APK vs AAB?
questions.a: An APK is installable as is. An AAB is a publishing format: Google Play generates optimised APKs per device from it and signs them. Play requires AAB for new apps. Testers outside Play need an APK.

questions.q: What is Play App Signing and the upload key?
questions.a: Google holds the app signing key and signs what users receive. The team signs uploads with a separate upload key. If the upload key is lost or leaked it can be reset through Google, which is not possible with a self-managed signing key.

questions.q: How do you keep the keystore out of the repo?
questions.a: Store the keystore as a Jenkins Secret file and the passwords and alias as Secret text, bind them in the build stage, and have build.gradle read them from environment variables or Gradle properties.

questions.q: Build type, flavor, variant?
questions.a: Build types describe how to build (debug, release). Product flavors describe what to build (qa, prod, brand). A variant is one combination, such as prodRelease, and has its own tasks like assembleProdRelease.

questions.q: What is mapping.txt?
questions.a: The R8 output that maps shortened class and method names back to the originals. It is needed to de-obfuscate release stack traces, so it is uploaded to the crash service and to Play and kept with the build.

questions.q: Why might you disable the Gradle daemon on CI?
questions.a: On shared or short-lived agents the daemon keeps memory after the build and brings little benefit. On a dedicated long-lived agent leaving it on speeds up the next build.

questions.q: How do you speed up Gradle builds on CI?
questions.a: Keep ~/.gradle caches, enable the build cache and configuration cache, set enough heap, enable parallel execution, avoid clean on non-release builds, and split checks into parallel stages.

questions.q: How do you guarantee versionCode increases?
questions.a: Derive it from CI (build number, commit count or timestamp) through a Gradle property, and keep exactly one job as the source for release uploads.

questions.q: Does the Android agent have to be a Mac?
questions.a: No. Android builds run on Linux, which allows Docker or Kubernetes agents that are cheap and disposable. Only iOS needs macOS.

questions.q: How is a Flutter module built in an add-to-app iOS project?
questions.a: flutter pub get generates the hidden .ios folder with podhelper.rb. The Podfile loads it and calls install_all_flutter_pods. During xcodebuild a script phase compiles the Dart code for the configuration. Alternatively flutter build ios-framework produces xcframeworks that the host links.

questions.q: What must CI do before pod install in such a project?
questions.a: Run flutter pub get in the module with the pinned Flutter version, otherwise the Podfile cannot load the Flutter helper.

questions.q: How do you pin the Flutter version on CI?
questions.a: FVM with a version file in the repo, or separate SDK folders per version selected through PATH. Print flutter --version in every build and commit pubspec.lock.

questions.q: Debug, profile and release mode on CI?
questions.a: Debug uses JIT with hot reload and is slow. Profile and release are AOT compiled. Tester and store builds must be release. In add-to-app the mode follows the Xcode configuration or Gradle build type.

questions.q: Source integration or prebuilt frameworks/AAR?
questions.a: Source keeps one build and is simple for teams that change Dart daily, but every machine needs Flutter and builds are longer. Prebuilt artifacts make native builds faster and Flutter-free, but add a pipeline that builds and versions them.

questions.q: How do you distribute test builds?
questions.a: iOS: ad hoc .ipa through Firebase App Distribution for registered devices, or TestFlight for wider groups. Android: APK through Firebase App Distribution, or Play internal testing. The pipeline uploads and posts the link with release notes to the team channel.

questions.q: Describe a release branch flow with CI.
questions.a: Cut a release branch, bump the version, every commit builds a candidate to TestFlight and Play internal, QA approves a build number, that exact binary is promoted to production with staged rollout, the commit is tagged, symbols are kept, and the branch is merged back.

questions.q: Why promote a binary instead of rebuilding for production?
questions.a: A rebuild is a different binary: dependencies or tools may have changed since QA tested. Promoting guarantees users get what was tested.

questions.q: How do you roll back a bad mobile release?
questions.a: You cannot pull a binary from phones. Halt the phased release or staged rollout, switch off the feature with a remote flag, and ship a hotfix build with a higher version. On iOS, ask for expedited review if needed.

questions.q: What belongs in a build notification?
questions.a: App, platform, branch, commit message, version and build number, result, install or console link, who triggered it. On failure, the stage that failed.

questions.q: Where does Jenkins keep its state and how do you back it up?
questions.a: In JENKINS_HOME: job configs, build records, plugins, credentials.xml and the secrets folder with the encryption keys. Back up the whole folder (build artifacts optional). Without the secrets folder the stored credentials cannot be decrypted.

questions.q: How do you upgrade Jenkins safely?
questions.a: Stay on the LTS line, read the upgrade guide and plugin advisories, back up JENKINS_HOME, put the server in quiet-down mode, upgrade core then plugins, run one build of each important job.

questions.q: How would you set up a Mac as an agent?
questions.a: Dedicated user with auto-login, agent started as a LaunchAgent in that session, sleep disabled, Xcode installed with licence accepted and first launch done, pinned Ruby, CocoaPods and Flutter, PATH set in node config, labels for what is installed, automatic OS updates off.

questions.q: The queue is always long. What do you do?
questions.a: Find out whether builds are slow or agents are few. Shorten builds with caching and by splitting stages, add agents or executors where hardware allows, cancel superseded PR builds, move non-Mac work to Linux agents, and run heavy jobs at night.

questions.q: What is Configuration as Code?
questions.a: A plugin that reads the server configuration (security, agents, credentials references, tools) from YAML in Git, so a server can be recreated and changes are reviewed.

questions.q: What are ephemeral agents and why use them?
questions.a: Agents created for one build and destroyed after: containers for Android, macOS virtual machines for iOS. Every build starts clean, images are versioned, and no secret or stale file survives between builds.

questions.q: How do you manage secrets in Jenkins?
questions.a: Jenkins Credentials store, scoped to folders, bound only around the steps that need them, never echoed, with low-privilege API keys, rotation on staff changes and an inventory with expiry dates. For larger setups, an external vault with short-lived secrets.

questions.q: Is log masking enough to protect a secret?
questions.a: No. It replaces only the exact string. Anyone who can change a job or Jenkinsfile that uses a credential can send it elsewhere or print it encoded. Protection comes from limiting who can configure jobs and edit protected branches.

questions.q: Why should the controller have zero executors?
questions.a: A build running on the controller can read JENKINS_HOME, including credential files and keys. Builds belong on agents.

questions.q: How do you protect release signing keys from PR builds?
questions.a: Keep them in a folder-scoped credential store used only by release jobs, never expose credentials to builds of fork pull requests, protect release branches, and run release jobs on dedicated agents.

questions.q: What is the script approval sandbox?
questions.a: Pipeline code from Git runs in a restricted Groovy sandbox. Calls outside an allow-list are blocked until an administrator approves them. It limits what a Jenkinsfile author can do on the controller.

questions.q: Build fails on Jenkins but works on your Mac. How do you approach it?
questions.a: Read the first error. Compare tool versions and environment between the two machines. Reproduce from a clean clone locally to rule out uncommitted or cached state. Then look at agent-only things: PATH, Xcode selection, keychain, profiles, disk space, concurrency.

questions.q: iOS builds started failing this morning with no code change.
questions.a: Suspect something time-based or external: an expired certificate or profile, an agent that auto-updated Xcode or macOS, an unpinned dependency release, a full disk, an expired token. Diff the version block and the first error against yesterday's green log.

questions.q: The iOS job takes 18 minutes. Bring it down.
questions.a: Measure per stage. Stop cleaning for debug builds, keep Pods and DerivedData, skip pod install when the lock matches, disable indexing, keep caches, run analysis and unit tests in parallel on another agent, consider prebuilt Flutter frameworks, and check the hardware.

questions.q: The distribution certificate expires in two weeks. Plan it.
questions.a: Create the new certificate now, regenerate all profiles including extensions, add them to Jenkins under new IDs, switch a debug job, then release jobs, verify an upload, update the calendar, and revoke the old certificate after a release ships on the new one.

questions.q: QA says the build they got does not contain the fix.
questions.a: Check the build page: branch parameter, commit hash, Changes list. Common causes: built the wrong branch, built before the merge, a cached workspace on an old commit, or QA installed an older build number. Put the commit hash and build number in the app's debug screen and in the notification.

questions.q: Design a mobile CI/CD system for a team of 30.
questions.a: PRs: multibranch pipeline with analyze, unit tests and an unsigned compile in under 15 minutes. Main: signed QA builds to Firebase on every merge. Release branches: candidates to TestFlight and Play internal, manual approval, promotion of the tested binary. Mac agents with one executor each or VM-based ephemeral agents, Linux containers for Android and Dart checks, secrets in folder-scoped credentials, pipeline and server config in Git, metrics on duration and failure causes.

questions.q: How would you migrate Freestyle jobs to Pipeline with no downtime?
questions.a: Move shell steps into scripts in the repo first, then write a Jenkinsfile calling them, run it as a parallel job, compare outputs for a while, switch the team over, disable then delete the old job.

questions.q: Someone committed the keystore password. What now?
questions.a: Treat it as leaked: rotate the password and, for an upload key, request an upload-key reset through Play. Remove it from history if policy requires, add secret scanning to PR checks, and move the value into Jenkins credentials.

questions.q: What is the difference between build, compile and archive?
questions.a: Compile turns source files into object code. Build does everything needed for a runnable product: compile, link, copy resources, sign. Archive is a build of the release kind for a real device, packaged with its debug symbols so it can be exported and distributed.

questions.q: What is a webhook and why is it better than polling?
questions.a: A webhook is an HTTP call the Git server makes to Jenkins the moment something happens. Polling asks the Git server on a timer. Webhooks start builds within seconds and cost nothing when idle; polling wastes requests and adds delay, but works when the Git server cannot reach Jenkins.

questions.q: What is the Jenkins REST API used for?
questions.a: Reading job and build state as JSON or XML and starting builds from scripts, chat bots or dashboards. Any page gets a machine form by adding /api/json. Calls authenticate with a user name and personal API token.

questions.q: LTS vs weekly Jenkins release?
questions.a: Weekly releases carry the newest changes. Long-Term Support releases are cut from a weekly about every twelve weeks and then receive only important fixes. Production servers use LTS for stability.

questions.q: What are upstream and downstream jobs?
questions.a: An upstream job triggers or feeds another; the triggered one is downstream. A build job that hands its .ipa to an automation job is the usual mobile example. Fingerprints let Jenkins show which builds are linked.

questions.q: How do you keep Jenkins from filling its disk?
questions.a: Build discarders on every job (keep a number of builds and fewer artifacts), workspace cleanup, artifacts stored outside the controller for long-term keeping, and disk monitoring on controller and agents.

questions.q: What is the difference between environment and parameters?
questions.a: Parameters are inputs chosen when a build starts. Environment entries are variables the pipeline defines for its steps, fixed or computed, including credentials. Parameters are also exposed as environment variables to shell steps.

questions.q: What does checkout scm do?
questions.a: It checks out the same repository and revision the Jenkinsfile itself was loaded from. In a Multibranch job that is the branch or pull request being built. In a job with an inline script there is no scm, so you call checkout with explicit settings.

questions.q: How do you run stages in parallel and when should you not?
questions.a: With a parallel block inside a stage, ideally each branch on its own agent. Avoid it for work that shares mutable state on one machine: two Xcode builds sharing DerivedData or a keychain, or two Gradle builds on a small agent.

questions.q: What is a matrix build?
questions.a: A declarative block that runs the same stages for every combination of axis values, such as flavor times build type, in parallel. It replaces copy-pasted stages.

questions.q: How do you fail a build on purpose, or mark it unstable?
questions.a: error("message") fails it. unstable("message") or catchError with buildResult UNSTABLE marks it unstable and continues. A non-zero exit code from sh fails the step unless returnStatus is used.

questions.q: What is the difference between returnStdout and returnStatus in sh?
questions.a: returnStdout gives the command output as a string for use in the pipeline. returnStatus gives the exit code and stops the step from failing the build, so the pipeline can branch on it.

questions.q: Why can a pipeline survive a controller restart, and what does that cost?
questions.a: Pipeline state is saved to disk after each step, so a run continues after a restart. The cost is that local variables must be serializable, which is where NotSerializableException comes from, and heavy Groovy logic in a pipeline is slow. Keep logic in shell scripts.

questions.q: How do you restart a failed pipeline from the middle?
questions.a: Declarative pipelines offer Restart from Stage on the build page. Files from earlier stages are available only if they were stashed with preserveStashes or still exist in the workspace.

questions.q: How do you pass data between stages?
questions.a: Environment variables set in a script block, files in the workspace when stages share an agent, stash and unstash across agents, and archived artifacts or parameters between separate jobs.

questions.q: What is the difference between agent any, none and label?
questions.a: any runs on whichever agent is free. none allocates nothing at the top so each stage declares its own agent, which is needed for input steps that should not hold a machine. label picks agents carrying that label.

questions.q: Target, scheme and build configuration: how do they relate?
questions.a: A target is one product with its settings. A build configuration is a named set of setting values such as Debug or Release. A scheme ties them together: for each action (run, archive and so on) it says which targets to build and which configuration to use.

questions.q: Which configuration does an archive use?
questions.a: The one set in the scheme under Archive, normally Release. The scheme name does not decide it. A scheme called Debug can still archive in Release, so always check the scheme or pass -configuration on purpose.

questions.q: What is an xcconfig file and why do CI engineers like it?
questions.a: A plain text file of build settings attached to a configuration. It keeps settings out of the project file, is easy to diff and review, and lets CI swap values such as signing or bundle IDs by supplying a different file.

questions.q: Why is passing PROVISIONING_PROFILE_SPECIFIER on the command line a problem?
questions.a: Command-line settings apply to every target in the build, including pods and extensions. Each needs a different profile or none, so one value breaks the others. Profiles must be set per target or through the export options map.

questions.q: What does -allowProvisioningUpdates do?
questions.a: It lets xcodebuild talk to the Apple developer service to create or update certificates, App IDs and profiles for automatically signed targets. On CI it needs credentials, normally an App Store Connect API key passed with the authenticationKey flags.

questions.q: What is a cloud-managed certificate?
questions.a: A distribution certificate whose private key Apple holds. Xcode asks Apple to sign during export instead of using a local key. With automatic signing and a suitably privileged API key, a CI machine can produce App Store builds with no .p12 installed.

questions.q: How do you build for the simulator on CI and why would you?
questions.a: xcodebuild build with a simulator destination and CODE_SIGNING_ALLOWED=NO. It needs no certificates, so it is the right compile check for pull requests and the base for unit and UI runs.

questions.q: What is bitcode and do you still need it?
questions.a: An intermediate form Apple could recompile. It was deprecated in Xcode 14 and is no longer accepted or needed. Old export option keys about bitcode can be removed.

questions.q: What is app thinning?
questions.a: Apple delivers to each device only the slices and resources it needs. The export step can produce thinned variants and a size report so the team sees per-device download size.

questions.q: Why does an iOS agent need a logged-in GUI session?
questions.a: Keychain access, code signing prompts, simulators and UI runs depend on a user session. A build started from a system daemon or a bare SSH session can fail to reach the login keychain or boot a simulator.

questions.q: How do you symbolicate a crash by hand?
questions.a: Match the build UUID in the crash report with dwarfdump --uuid on the dSYM, then use atos with the load address, or drop the report into Xcode Organizer with the archive present.

questions.q: What is a privacy manifest?
questions.a: A PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy file in the app and in SDKs that declares collected data and the reasons for using certain APIs. Uploads without required entries get warning or rejection emails from App Store Connect.

questions.q: What is notarization and does an iOS app need it?
questions.a: Notarization is Apple's automated check for macOS software distributed outside the Mac App Store. iOS apps do not go through it; they are checked by App Store processing and review.

questions.q: An extension was added and the CI export broke. Why?
questions.a: The new target needs its own App ID and distribution profile, a development team in every configuration, a line in the export options profile map when signing manually, and the same version numbers as the app.

questions.q: How does Gradle find signing details on CI without storing them in the repo?
questions.a: From Gradle properties supplied at build time: -P flags, environment variables named ORG_GRADLE_PROJECT_name, or a properties file written by the job. They override values in gradle.properties.

questions.q: What is the Gradle wrapper and why commit it?
questions.a: A small script and jar that download and run one exact Gradle version. Committing it means every developer and CI machine builds with the same Gradle and nobody installs it by hand.

questions.q: What are R8 and ProGuard rules?
questions.a: R8 shrinks, optimises and renames code in minified builds. Keep rules tell it what must not be removed or renamed, typically classes used through reflection or serialization. Missing rules cause crashes that appear only in minified builds.

questions.q: What are APK signature schemes v1 to v4?
questions.a: v1 signs individual files and is needed only for very old Android. v2 signs the whole file, v3 adds key rotation, v4 supports incremental install. apksigner verify shows which are present.

questions.q: What is the difference between assemble, bundle and install tasks?
questions.a: assemble builds APKs, bundle builds an app bundle for Play, install builds and pushes an APK to a connected device. Each exists per variant.

questions.q: How do you run instrumented checks on CI?
questions.a: On an emulator started headless on the agent, on Gradle Managed Devices, or on a device farm. The emulator needs hardware acceleration, so it usually runs on bare-metal or specially enabled machines.

questions.q: What is a version catalog?
questions.a: A libs.versions.toml file that lists dependency coordinates and versions in one place for all modules, so upgrades are single-line changes and reviewable.

questions.q: A release build works locally but fails on Jenkins with out of memory. What do you check?
questions.a: Agent RAM against org.gradle.jvmargs, number of parallel workers, other builds running on the same agent, whether the daemon from an earlier build is still holding memory, and container memory limits if it runs in Docker.

questions.q: Why can a tester not open a debug-mode Flutter build from the home screen?
questions.a: Debug mode uses JIT compilation, which recent iOS versions allow only with a debugger attached. Tester builds must be release mode, which is AOT compiled.

questions.q: What does pubspec.lock do and should it be committed?
questions.a: It records the exact version of every Dart package resolved. For apps and modules it should be committed so CI and all developers get identical dependencies.

questions.q: How do you read an obfuscated Dart stack trace?
questions.a: With the symbol files written by --split-debug-info for that exact build, using flutter symbolize or the crash service after uploading them. Without those files the trace cannot be decoded.

questions.q: What changes in CI when Flutter is embedded from source instead of as binaries?
questions.a: Every native build needs the Flutter SDK at the right version, must run flutter pub get first, and compiles Dart during the native build, which takes longer. In exchange there is one pipeline and no separate artifact to version.

questions.q: What is semantic versioning and how do mobile teams bend it?
questions.a: Major.minor.patch, where the parts signal breaking changes, features and fixes. Apps have no API consumers, so teams usually bump minor per release train and patch for hotfixes, with a separate always-increasing build number.

questions.q: What is a release train?
questions.a: Releases leave on a fixed schedule, for example every two weeks. Whatever is ready ships; what is not waits for the next one. It removes negotiation about dates and makes CI cadence predictable.

questions.q: How do feature flags change the release pipeline?
questions.a: Code ships switched off and is turned on remotely, so merging and releasing are separate decisions. Rollback becomes a flag change. The pipeline still has to exercise both states.

questions.q: What is the difference between internal, closed, open and production tracks on Play?
questions.a: Internal reaches up to a hundred named testers within minutes. Closed goes to invited lists. Open is a public beta. Production is everyone, optionally by staged percentage. A build is promoted from one track to the next without re-uploading.

questions.q: SSH agent or inbound agent for a Mac?
questions.a: Inbound, started as a LaunchAgent in the logged-in session, so builds have keychain and simulator access and the connection works outbound through firewalls. SSH agents are simpler but run outside the GUI session.

questions.q: How do you roll out a new Xcode to build agents?
questions.a: Install it beside the old one, add a new label, point one non-critical job at it with DEVELOPER_DIR, fix what breaks, then move jobs over and remove the old version after a release has shipped from the new one.

questions.q: Which metrics tell you a CI system is healthy?
questions.a: Success rate, median and tail build time, queue wait time, share of failures caused by infrastructure and not code, and how long the main branch stays red.

questions.q: A plugin update broke the server. How do you recover?
questions.a: Restore the previous plugin file from the backup or use the downgrade button in the plugin manager, restart, and next time update on a copy of the server first. Keep JENKINS_HOME backups from before every update.

questions.q: What is the risk of building pull requests from forks?
questions.a: The pull request can change the Jenkinsfile or build scripts and so run any code on the agent. If credentials are available it can steal them. Fork builds should run with no secrets, on isolated agents, or only after a maintainer approves.

questions.q: How would you audit who can ship the app?
questions.a: List who can configure release jobs, who can push to release branches and to the shared pipeline library, who has admin on Jenkins, who holds store roles and API keys, and who can log into the build Macs. All of those can reach the signing keys.

questions.q: Why prefer short-lived credentials?
questions.a: A leaked long-lived key works until someone notices. Short-lived tokens from a vault or identity federation expire on their own and are tied to one job, which limits damage.

questions.q: The debug job is named Debug but testers say the build behaves like production. What do you check?
questions.a: The scheme's Archive configuration, since a scheme named Debug may archive in Release; the bundle ID and API host baked in for that configuration; and the Flutter build mode. Then decide whether the job or the scheme should change.

questions.q: Jenkins has two executors and iOS builds queue all day. What do you propose?
questions.a: Measure where time goes, shorten the build with caches and by skipping clean, move Android and Dart checks to a Linux agent, add a second Mac, cancel superseded builds of the same branch, and schedule long jobs overnight.

questions.q: You must add a third app target (a new brand) to CI. What is the list?
questions.a: New App IDs and profiles for the app and each extension, Firebase and push setup, a scheme that is shared, export options for it, a job parameter or matrix axis, store listings and API access, and symbols and notifications wired like the others.

questions.q: A build is green but the uploaded app crashes on launch for testers. Where do you look?
questions.a: Signing and entitlements of the exported .ipa, missing or wrong configuration files for that environment, a release-only code path such as minification or AOT, and the crash report symbolicated with that build's dSYM. Then add a launch smoke check to the pipeline.

questions.q: How do you introduce CI changes without breaking the team?
questions.a: Work on a copy of the job, keep the old one running, compare outputs, announce the switch, keep a rollback, and change one thing at a time so a failure has one suspect.
